t: Introduction: topic, aim and plan
n: In this lecture we consider questions of reproductive ethics. In the twentieth century biology and medicine developed rapidly. It is now possible to intervene in the beginning of human life, and this has given rise to new ethical problems. If new technologies are applied without control and without moral norms, they may affect the individual and later generations and damage family relationships. Reproductive ethics is a part of bioethics that studies the ethical problems of intervention in human reproduction. The plan: abortion, ART, that is, assisted reproductive technologies, surrogacy, embryo research, prenatal diagnosis, eugenics and sterilisation.

t: The moral status of the embryo and foetus
n: First let us consider the moral status of the embryo and foetus. The as yet unborn living being, that is, the embryo or foetus, is not a part of the woman's body. It is regarded as a socially recognised subject of moral relations. Therefore it is very important to determine the socially recognised boundary at which the embryo and foetus possess a human essence. Determining this status is closely tied to the resolution of the question of terminating pregnancy. In the second trimester, that is, months 4 to 6, a reaction to various influences is formed. For this reason some consider abortion permissible at an early stage, mainly in the first trimester.

t: Two approaches: person or potential person
n: There are two approaches to the status of the embryo. The first regards the embryo as a person, the second as a potential person. Supporters of preserving life call the embryo a person and give it the moral status proper to a person. Supporters of free choice regard the embryo only as a potential person and do not recognise such a status before birth. Remember: a potential person is not the same as an actual person. The main difference in the dispute lies precisely here.

t: Islam and assisted reproductive technologies
n: Now Islam and assisted reproductive technologies. According to a fatwa of the Muslim Board of Uzbekistan, artificial insemination is permissible only in necessary cases, for a married couple in accordance with Muslim custom. In vitro fertilisation is considered lawful only when the spermatozoa of the woman's husband are used. For couples not in a marriage under Sharia, artificial insemination is forbidden, and so that the seed of others is not mixed, all precautions are taken. If the egg does not belong to the husband's wife, or if the child is carried by an outside woman, Islam forbids this method. Permission also requires voluntary and conscious consent.

t: Time of the soul's entry into the body in religions
n: In religions, abortion is linked with the entry of the soul into the body, and until that time it is permitted in exceptional cases. The times differ. In the Church of England it is day 16, in Judaism day 40, in Christianity from fertilisation. In Islam the sources vary: on p. 87 month 4 is given, on p. 102 month 5. It should also be said that the main religious confessions are on the whole negative towards abortion.

t: Historical stages of attitudes to abortion
n: Let us consider the historical stages of attitudes to abortion. Hippocrates imposed a strict prohibition. Aristotle, for demographic purposes, spoke of performing abortion before sensation and motor activity have formed in the foetus. In Rome the foetus was regarded as part of the mother's body. In the Christian era the foetus came to be valued. In the sixteenth century the “Carolina” code in Germany set the death penalty for abortion. In 1852, in a discussion at the Paris Academy of Medicine, the conclusion was reached that abortion is possible on medical indication.

t: The nineteenth and twentieth centuries: bans, laws, liberalisation
n: In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries bans, laws and liberalisation succeeded one another. In the USA abortion was banned in 1880, with permission when the mother's life was at risk. The British Act of 1869 deemed even early abortion a grave crime. In the twentieth century the feminist movement played the main role in the debate. M. Sanger introduced the concept of “birth control”, later also used in a eugenic sense. In the former Union abortion was permitted in 1920, then banned, and in 1955 the ban was lifted and women could have an abortion at their own wish up to week 12. In December 2020 the Argentine Senate permitted abortion at the woman's wish up to week 14.

t: Quick question: history of abortion and status
n: Let us reinforce the topic with quick questions. When does the soul enter the body according to the Church of England and Islam? In the Church of England on day 16, in Islam in month 4. When was abortion permitted in the former Union? In 1920. The ban was lifted in 1955, at the woman's wish up to week 12. Up to what limit did the Argentine Senate permit abortion? In December 2020, up to week 14. Attention, there is a risk of error: a person is not the same as a potential person. Supporters of protecting life regard the embryo as a person, while supporters of free choice regard it only as a potential person.

t: Three positions on abortion
n: There are three positions on abortion. The liberal position demands that abortion be permitted, because the woman is mistress of her own body. The conservative position calls for abortion to be banned, because the embryo is a person and the complications are serious. The intermediate position holds abortion possible only on medical or social indication and does not endorse it as a woman's right. According to the WHO, about 70 thousand women die each year from abortion complications. In the world, for every 1000 women there are 30 unsafe abortions a year. For conservatives the key question is determining the viability of the foetus.

t: The pro-life movement and religious views
n: “Pro-life”, that is, the protection of life, is a social movement aimed at banning abortion on account of the unborn child's right to life. In the social concept of the Russian Orthodox Church, abortion is a grave sin equated with murder. This document states that types of IVF that involve destroying “surplus” embryos, and fetal therapy, are unacceptable. In Islam, abortion after 120 days of pregnancy is absolutely forbidden, and most jurists permit it up to 40 days. If the mother's life is in danger, an exception is made.

t: Case analysis: a clash of positions
n: Now a case analysis. A woman is considering having an abortion in unsafe conditions. How will the three positions answer her? In the liberal position the woman is mistress of her own body, the decision is autonomous, and if necessary the woman's life is preserved, not the foetus's. In the conservative position the embryo is a person, and abortion must be banned. According to the WHO, abortion complications lead to the deaths of women. In the intermediate position abortion is possible only on medical or social indication. Question: which position puts the woman's safety first?

t: Abortion models in Western Europe
n: There are three models of abortion in Western Europe. Complete prohibition, in Ireland and Poland: an exception when life is at risk, and in Poland also for rape and incest. In Poland in 2021 abortion is not possible even where the foetus has a defect such as Down syndrome. A system of indications, in Great Britain: abortion is permitted on a clear list of indications, that is, risk to life, genetic reasons and health. A system of time limits, in Austria, France and Norway: up to a time limit the woman's wish decides. Remember: in one model the reason decides, in the other the time limit.

t: Gestational limits and indications for abortion in Uzbekistan
n: The gestational limits and indications for abortion in Uzbekistan are as follows. First the absence of contraindications is established. After that, up to 12 weeks abortion is performed at the woman's wish. On social indication, up to 22 weeks, and on medical indication regardless of gestational age. The list of indications is given in the relevant legislation.

t: Complications and risk of abortion
n: Let us speak of the complications and risk of abortion. Because abortion is simple, convenient and free of charge, the mistaken notion arises that it is safe. The consequences: problems in the course of a subsequent pregnancy and delivery, various gynaecological diseases, inflammation and infertility. During abortion, complications of anaesthesia, perforation of the uterus, and external and internal bleeding are possible. In women who have had an abortion before, babies are more often born with defects, in severe asphyxia, or stillborn.

t: Contraception and the 1994 WMA statement
n: Contraceptives raise some ethical and religious problems, but they prevent unwanted pregnancy and reduce the number of abortions. In September 1994, at its 46th Assembly, the World Medical Association, that is, the WMA, adopted a statement on women's right to use contraceptives. The statement recognises the ability to regulate fertility as an important part of preserving a woman's physical and mental health and social well-being. In the WMA's view, all women, regardless of nationality, religion and social status, should have the right to use contraceptives on the basis of informed choice.

t: Articles 114 and 115 of the Criminal Code
n: Let us look at Articles 114 and 115 of the Criminal Code. Article 114: termination of pregnancy by an obstetrician-gynaecologist outside an institution or where medically impossible is regarded as criminal abortion. Cases of prohibition: inflammation of the genital organs, purulent foci, acute infectious diseases, a gestational age over 12 weeks; and also within six months of a previous abortion. In criminal abortion the gestational age and the method do not matter. If a pregnant woman terminates the pregnancy herself or other persons do so, the woman herself is not held criminally liable. Coercing a woman into artificial termination of pregnancy is also a crime; this is Article 115.

t: Case analysis: lawful and criminal abortion
n: Case analysis. A person who is not an obstetrician or gynaecologist terminated a woman's pregnancy outside a medical institution. The woman herself had agreed to it. Analysis: such an act by a person without the right to do so, and termination outside an institution, is regarded as criminal abortion under Article 114. The gestational age and method do not matter. The woman is not held criminally liable; responsibility lies with the person who terminated the pregnancy. Attention, there is a risk of error: lawful abortion, that is, up to 12 weeks in an institution, is not the same as criminal abortion, that is, under Article 114. Question: which article would be added if pressure had been put on the woman?

t: Reproductive health, rights and the concept of ART
n: According to Article 3 of the 2019 law, reproductive health is physical, mental and social well-being connected with the reproductive system and its function. The rights are: an independent decision to have a child by means of safe technology, reliable information, and the use of contraception and ART. Legal entities and individuals keep confidential information about a citizen's reproductive rights. No one may be coerced into pregnancy, abortion or contraception. Reproductive ethics is a part of bioethics. ART, that is, assisted reproductive technologies, is biomedical intervention in fertilisation and the development of the embryo.

t: Types of ART approved in Uzbekistan
n: Paragraph 14 of the Ministry of Health regulation names five ART methods. They are: insemination, that is, artificial insemination, in which sperm is introduced into the uterine cavity. IVF, that is, in vitro fertilisation, in which fertilisation takes place outside the body. Hatching and ICSI: opening the shell and introducing a spermatozoon. Cryopreservation, that is, freezing of gametes for storage. Surrogacy is not named in this regulation. Attention: ART is a general name, while methods such as IVF and ICSI are its separate types.

t: Artificial insemination: homologous and heterologous
n: Artificial insemination may be homologous or heterologous. A spermatozoon from the husband or from another man, a donor, is introduced into the woman's uterine cavity. In the homologous method the source of sperm is the husband, so no serious ethical problem arises. In the heterologous method the source of sperm is a male donor, the main ethical problems arise precisely with this method, and the biological father differs from the social father. If a donor is chosen, the child can be selected “to order” according to the donor's characteristics. Remember: homologous is not the same as heterologous.

t: Quick question: abortion laws and ART
n: Quick questions. Up to how many weeks is abortion possible at the woman's wish? Up to 12 weeks; on social indication up to 22 weeks, on medical indication regardless of gestational age. What do Articles 114 and 115 of the Criminal Code treat as crimes? Unlawful termination of pregnancy and coercing a woman into terminating pregnancy. What is the difference between homologous and heterologous insemination? In the first the husband's sperm is used, in the second the donor's; the main ethical problem lies in the heterologous type. Attention: in vitro fertilisation, that is, IVF, is not the same as surrogacy. Surrogacy is not named in the regulation on ART.

t: Stages of IVF
n: The stages of IVF are as follows. First ovarian hyperstimulation is carried out, then the egg is retrieved. Then sperm is selected and fertilisation is carried out, the embryo is grown in an incubator and finally transferred to the uterus. In hyperstimulation several eggs mature at once; this is done to guarantee the result. IVF is used in male and female infertility; fertilisation and early development take place outside the woman's body. In multiple pregnancy, surplus embryos are eliminated under ultrasound guidance; this is called reduction.

t: History and statistics of IVF
n: History and statistics of IVF. The first successful IVF was carried out by Robert Edwards and Patrick Christopher Steptoe. The egg was fertilised in 1968, Louise Brown was born in 1978, and Edwards received the Nobel Prize in 2010. Children born through IVF number more than 5 million. Now about 1.5 million IVF cycles are performed in the world each year; 23 to 25 per cent of them are successful. IVF is used mainly in women aged 30 to 39; more than half of world IVF falls to Europe.

t: IVF: main moral and ethical problems
n: The main moral and ethical problems of IVF. Pregnancy arises without sexual intercourse, and the child has a genetic father in addition to the social father. In hyperstimulation up to 10 eggs are sometimes retrieved. Surplus embryos may be destroyed; some call reduction “abortion by selection”. Pre-implantation testing makes it possible to discriminate against the child by sex and other characteristics. Frozen embryos may be used for industrial purposes. Here there is the problem of “woman as incubator” and the risk of the rarely occurring genetic incest.

t: IVF: medical problems
n: IVF has medical problems as well. To obtain a mature egg, ovulation is provoked. This may lead to ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome, which is dangerous for the woman. When the egg is cleaned mechanically and chemically, the zona pellucida may be damaged, and this may lead to neoplastic changes in the embryo. The spermatozoon bypasses the natural multi-stage selection, with the result that the rate of transmission of hereditary diseases to the child rises. In the first days the embryo develops outside the body, and therefore it is deprived of many natural internal factors.

t: IVF legislation and ethical recommendations
n: IVF legislation and ethical recommendations. In some countries reduction is banned or restricted, and the number of embryos transferred is limited. In Italy only the gametes of the spouses are used. In Germany and Costa Rica IVF is prohibited by law. In Russia sex selection is restricted, no more than two embryos are transferred, and reduction is carried out with the woman's informed consent. Mitigating recommendations: cautious stimulation, transfer of fewer embryos, free donation of surplus ones. Embryos must not be grown for industrial purposes; full information must be given before IVF.

t: Case analysis: surplus embryos
n: Case analysis. In a couple, several eggs, sometimes up to 10, were retrieved through hyperstimulation and fertilised; surplus embryos appeared. The problem: surplus embryos may be destroyed or used for other purposes. If the embryo is regarded as the seed of life, this is a serious moral question. Recommendations: cautious stimulation, free donation of surplus embryos to infertile couples without destroying them, and transfer of fewer embryos to the uterus. Question: in multiple pregnancy some researchers call reduction abortion by selection. In Russia no more than two embryos are transferred. Which solution is acceptable?

t: Cryopreservation, hatching and ICSI
n: Cryopreservation, hatching and ICSI. Cryopreservation is a freezing method in which gametes, embryos and gonadal tissue are stored in liquid nitrogen. Gametes and embryos are stored in specially labelled containers; the period is up to 10 years and more. Hatching is the opening of the zona pellucida, indicated at age 35 and over or after 3 or more unsuccessful attempts. Intracytoplasmic injection, that is, ICSI, is the introduction of a spermatozoon into the oocyte; the indication is impaired spermatogenesis and fewer than 4 oocytes. Emma, 2017, and Molly, 2020, are genetic sisters born from embryos frozen in 1992. All procedures are carried out on the basis of the informed consent of citizens.

t: Surrogacy: essence and types
n: The essence and types of surrogacy. The genetic mother provides the egg, while the surrogate mother carries the foetus and gives birth. If the egg is taken from the surrogate, this is partial surrogacy. The process is as follows: the genetic mother's egg is fertilised in vitro, the embryo is transferred into the surrogate mother's uterus, the surrogate mother carries the foetus, and the child is handed to the genetic mother. Consent may be commercial, that is, for money, or altruistic, that is, help from a relative or friend. Indications: uterine defect, scar and adhesion changes, internal diseases that prevent pregnancy.

t: Two cases of surrogacy
n: In the 1960s the era of artificial insemination began, and new ethical problems such as surrogacy arose. There are two cases of surrogacy. In the first, the surrogate mother carries the child of the genetic parents; if she does not want to hand the child over, conflict arises. In the second, a woman bears a child by an anonymous father; the donor's anonymity creates the risk of marriage between blood relatives. The concepts of family, motherhood and fatherhood also change: modern childbearing practice alters the traditional family system.

t: Moral and legal problems of surrogacy
n: Moral and legal problems of surrogacy. The integrity of the family is broken: another woman enters the family circle from outside, and the traditional notion of family values is undermined. The genetic mother and the surrogate mother are distinguished. Usually the biological mother is regarded as the woman who carried and gave birth to the foetus, that is, the surrogate mother. Article 207 of the Family Code: if a married couple consent to the transfer of the embryo to another woman, the consent of the woman who gave birth is required for them to be registered as parents. The number of parents may increase to five. Paid surrogacy commercialises the birth of a child, and the woman is likened to a commodity, an incubator.

t: Surrogacy: prohibition, requirements and the 1987 WMA statement
n: Surrogacy is banned in some countries: in Austria, Germany and France. Where it is permitted, the surrogate mother must be healthy, aged 20 to 35, with at least one healthy child. In Russia it is permitted, including for payment: age 20 to 30, at least one healthy child, a medical opinion. A surrogate mother is forbidden to be an egg donor at the same time. In Uzbekistan, surrogacy is not named in the regulation on assisted reproductive technologies approved by the Ministry of Health. The WMA statement of 1987, Madrid: if infertility cannot be treated otherwise, the methods are justified; paid surrogacy is rejected, as is trade in gametes and embryos.

t: Quick question: IVF, surrogacy
n: Quick questions. First question: what are the 6 stages of IVF? Hyperstimulation, egg retrieval, sperm selection, fertilisation, growth in an incubator, transfer to the uterus. Second question: what is the difference between hatching and ICSI? Hatching is the opening of the zona pellucida, while ICSI is the introduction of a spermatozoon into the cytoplasm of the oocyte. Third question: what forms does surrogacy take? If the egg is taken from the surrogate mother, it is partial surrogacy; consent is given on a commercial or an altruistic, that is, unpaid, basis. Attention: the genetic mother is not the same as the biological mother. Usually the biological mother is regarded as the woman who gave birth, that is, the surrogate mother, not the owner of the egg.

t: Research on embryos: the Oviedo Convention
n: Research on embryos and the Oviedo Convention. Views on the entry of the soul: in Islam month 5, in Judaism day 40, in Christianity immediately on fertilisation of the egg. The Council of Europe's Oviedo Convention of 1997 prohibits creating embryos for research. The additional protocol of 1998 banned human cloning. By their approaches, states fall into three groups. The USA, Norway and Switzerland are in the first group, with a strict ban. Australia and Great Britain are in the second group, on the basis of law. Spain and Sweden are also in the second group, up to day 14.

t: Prenatal diagnosis: ethical questions
n: Prenatal diagnosis makes it possible to detect chromosomal diseases, sex-linked diseases and congenital defects. The ethical basis: it allows doubtful parents to be sure that the child is healthy. Opponents above all accuse it of providing grounds for abortion; the question of choosing abortion when a disease treatable with drugs is found has not been resolved. In genetic counselling the physician must take a morally neutral position: the patients themselves make the decision.

t: Moratorium and regulation: lessons of cloning
n: Moratorium and regulation, lessons of cloning. The additional protocol of the Council of Europe bans human cloning; this showed the need for a legal definition of the concept “human being”. Scientific thought cannot be banned: in the 1940s to 60s genetics and cybernetics were banned; the application of achievements needs to be regulated. How does society decide on something new? First open discussion, in which any point of view is given a voice. The decision rests not on feelings but on knowledge. The morality of citizens and the preparation of specialists are assessed. If society is not ready, a moratorium is introduced, educational work is carried out, and the question is revisited.

t: Case analysis: research on a 14-day embryo
n: Case analysis. In a laboratory in Spain an egg has been fertilised, day 14 has not yet passed, and a diagnostic procedure is planned. If the same plan were in the USA, Norway or Switzerland, the research would fall into the group of strict prohibition. Question: is it permissible to create a new embryo solely for research? How does the Oviedo Convention regard this? Attention, there is a risk of error: the 14-day allowance does not apply everywhere; in some countries there is a ban.

t: Prenatal diagnosis and the concept of eugenics
n: Prenatal diagnosis and the concept of eugenics. Chorionic biopsy is an invasive method: villi are taken at weeks 9 to 11. Cytogenetic analysis shows chromosomal disease and sex; written consent is obtained. In 1883 Galton called eugenics the study of factors influencing the qualities of offspring. Muller's criteria: intelligence, organisation, health. In the USA and Germany eugenics led to compulsory sterilisation, racist ideas and the crimes of fascism. Present-day problems of prenatal selection: should one give birth when there is a risk, should pregnancy be terminated if the foetus is ill, should one consent to donor sperm?

t: Sterilisation: negative and positive eugenics
n: Sterilisation: negative and positive eugenics. Negative eugenics tries to improve heredity by sterilisation, positive eugenics by encouragement and selection. Timeline: in 1883 Galton proposed the term “eugenics”; in 1907 Indiana passed a compulsory sterilisation law; in 1933 Hitler came to power and racism intensified; in 1937 the last law was passed in Georgia. While compulsory sterilisation laws were in force in the USA, more than 100 thousand people were sterilised. An example of positive eugenics: R. Graham set up a bank to store the sperm of Nobel laureates.

t: Case analysis: compulsory sterilisation
n: Case analysis. The 1907 Indiana law provided for the sterilisation of the mentally ill, the intellectually disabled, chronic alcoholics, orphans and others. The last law was passed in 1937 in Georgia. Many Black people were also sterilised by force. In Germany after 1933 racism became a state programme, and the mentally ill and people of mixed race were sterilised. Question: why is sterilisation by state decision regarded as an impermissible interference in human life?

t: Conclusion: key principles and review questions
n: Let us conclude. On the status of the embryo, supporters of preserving life call the embryo a person, while supporters of free choice regard it only as a potential person. On abortion there are liberal, conservative and intermediate positions. In Uzbekistan it is possible at the woman's wish up to 12 weeks, and on social indication up to 22 weeks. In assisted reproductive technologies, that is, ART, in in vitro fertilisation, IVF, the problem is surplus embryos; in surrogacy, the problem of the mother's identity and of commercialisation. Lessons of eugenics: compulsory sterilisation leads to abuse. Attention: negative eugenics is not the same as positive eugenics.
